paragraphs: Ambient Dataloops addresses a problem in generative modeling: training examples can differ substantially in quality, making their underlying distribution harder to learn. The paper proposes improving the dataset and the diffusion model together through repeated rounds of refinement. Each round uses synthetic improvements to produce a higher-quality dataset, which then supports further model improvement.

The central design choice concerns how the method treats its own generated data. It regards improved samples as still corrupted, with slightly less noise than in the preceding round. Ambient Diffusion provides the machinery for learning from these imperfect samples. This treatment is intended to avoid destructive feedback loops in which repeatedly consuming synthetic data undermines the model.

The authors report state-of-the-art empirical performance for image generation both with and without text conditioning, and for designing new proteins. They also provide a theoretical justification capturing benefits of the iterative procedure. The contribution therefore combines a dataset-refinement strategy with a way to account for the continuing imperfections of synthetic training examples.
icml-2026-ambient-dataloops-generative-m.tldr: Ambient Dataloops repeatedly improves datasets and diffusion models while treating synthetic refinements as imperfect observations.

paragraphs: AOrchestra addresses how an AI system should delegate parts of a complex, extended task. Existing sub-agent arrangements can provide isolated conversation threads without much specialization, or fixed roles that people must design in advance. The paper introduces a common description of an agent using four components: its model, task, tools, and context.

A central orchestrator fills in these components as work proceeds. It selects relevant information, chooses a model and tools, and creates a specialized executor for the current task. This makes agent creation part of the system’s ongoing decisions. The abstraction is intended to work across frameworks and accommodate different kinds of executors with less human engineering.

The design also makes performance and computational cost controllable through these choices, allowing the system to approach efficient trade-offs. Across GAIA, SWE-Bench, and Terminal-Bench, the authors report a 16.28% relative improvement over the strongest baseline when using Gemini-3-Flash. This result supports the proposed approach in the evaluated settings; it is specifically tied to that model pairing.
icml-2026-aorchestra-automating-sub-agen.tldr: AOrchestra creates specialized sub-agents on demand by choosing their models, tasks, tools, and context during execution.

paragraphs: When language models judge responses, they sometimes favor answers they produced themselves. This paper examines whether that pattern necessarily reflects a preference for their own authorship. A judge that struggles with a question may also judge its answers poorly, creating apparent self-preference that can be explained by evaluator quality.

The authors introduce a baseline that directly compares the judge’s voting distribution when evaluating itself with its voting distribution when evaluating another model. This comparison tests whether the observed behavior exceeds what the evaluator-quality explanation would predict. It makes the interpretation of self-preference depend on a relevant alternative explanation, rather than on the direction of the verdict alone.

Under this baseline, 51% of examples from previous findings remain statistically significant, accounting for 89.6% of total self-preference probability mass. These figures show that many individual findings weaken while much of the probability mass remains. An additional comparison of voting entropy suggests overlap driven by uncertainty. The procedure supports more careful documentation of judge bias without dismissing the remaining evidence.
icml-2026-are-llm-evaluators-really-narc.tldr: An evaluator-quality baseline weakens many reported self-preference findings while retaining most of their total probability mass.

paragraphs: The paper connects softmax attention with Bayesian inference through their shared use of normalization. For finite latent categories and observations from exponential families, it proves that one attention head can exactly compute posterior probabilities and posterior means. It also characterizes the posteriors available to a single head: they are precisely those with a log-linear form.

The next question is geometric: when can this Bayesian interpretation use one quadratic distance measure everywhere? Using an established exponential-family identity, the authors show that this is possible exactly when the relevant dual potential is quadratic. When curvature changes across the space, they construct a multi-head collection of local approximations and provide bounds on approximation accuracy and the number of heads.

The analysis extends to in-context estimation, including consistency, finite-sample stability, and a connection between excess prediction loss and approximate key-subspace alignment. Controlled Gaussian, Bernoulli, and Poisson diagnostics illustrate the different regimes. The exact results concern finite discrete latent classes; their implications for larger learned transformers are presented as testable predictions, not universal descriptions.
icml-2026-attention-implements-the-fishe.tldr: For finite latent classes, attention can implement exact Bayesian inference, with geometric conditions explaining when one shared metric suffices.

paragraphs: Predicting how genetic interventions change a cell requires accounting for genes that respond together. The paper argues that treating genes independently, or relying on fixed biological relationships, misses coordinated changes in gene programs. Its proposed framework, scBIG, learns representations organized around these programs so that predictions can reflect relationships among groups of genes.

The method first discovers coherent programs from data through Gene-Relation Clustering. A Gene-Cluster-Aware Encoder then represents interactions between programs, while structure-aware alignment objectives help preserve their internal coordination. Conditional flow matching models the resulting structured representations to predict responses to perturbations. Together, these components make coordinated gene behavior an explicit part of the prediction process.

Across multiple single-cell perturbation benchmarks, the authors report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, averaging 6.7% over the strongest baselines. The gains are particularly pronounced for previously unseen interventions and combinations of interventions. These findings support the value of learning gene-program structure when the prediction task requires generalizing beyond perturbations already represented in training.
icml-2026-beyond-independent-genes-learn.tldr: scBIG learns coordinated gene programs to improve predictions of cellular responses, especially for unseen and combined genetic perturbations.

paragraphs: Categorical Flow Maps aims to generate categorical data in very few computational steps. The paper develops a flow-matching method with self-distillation, allowing the model to learn accelerated generation. Its central construction moves probability mass toward a predicted endpoint on the probability simplex, the space of valid probability distributions over categories.

Although the outputs are categorical, the paths used by the method are continuous. This choice makes existing distillation techniques usable and supports a new training objective based on endpoint consistency. The parameterization also naturally constrains predictions. These properties connect the categorical generation problem to tools already available for accelerating continuous diffusion and flow models.

The continuous formulation additionally allows guidance and reweighting techniques to steer generation toward downstream objectives at test time. Empirically, the authors report state-of-the-art few-step results for images, molecular graphs, and text, with strong performance even from a single generation step. The contribution brings accelerated sampling and test-time steering into the same framework for these different forms of categorical data.
icml-2026-categorical-flow-maps-817df6ea.tldr: Categorical Flow Maps uses continuous probability trajectories and self-distillation for fast, steerable categorical generation.

paragraphs: This paper studies which training examples diffusion models memorize first. The authors train models on strings produced by the Random Hierarchy Model, which provides structured production rules. In this setting, examples assembled from common substrings are preferentially memorized. The findings challenge the idea that rare or atypical examples must be the earliest targets of memorization.

The effect remains when every complete training example is unique. Removing duplicate examples therefore does not provide a meaningful privacy guarantee in the studied setting, because shared pieces can still be memorized. The authors also predict and observe later memorization in datasets with more atypical samples. Introducing this diversity into higher-level production rules strengthens the delay.

An intermediate stage reveals partial memorization: common substrings are learned first and then generated too often. Stopping training during this stage produces the bland, average-seeking outputs discussed in the title. Together, the results suggest that dataset diversity, especially in higher-level structure, can help delay memorization and explain why repetitive generation may emerge before complete examples are memorized.
icml-2026-diffusion-models-preferentiall.tldr: In structured-string experiments, diffusion models memorize common patterns first, while greater high-level diversity delays memorization.

paragraphs: The paper studies multi-agent decision-making when the environment’s dynamics may differ from the assumed model. Its framework combines distributional robustness with an average-reward objective, focusing on performance over extended operation. A central question is whether the players can reach a Nash equilibrium, where their policies are mutual best responses.

Under a standard irreducibility assumption, the authors connect optimal policies to solutions of a robust Bellman equation and establish the existence of a stationary equilibrium. They then consider the more general weakly communicating setting. There, they construct a set-valued map whose outputs belong to the best-response policies and prove that it has a fixed point, establishing equilibrium existence through a different route.

The authors also introduce Robust Nash-Iteration and robust TD Descent, with convergence guarantees. Finally, they show that equilibria of discounted robust games can approximate average-reward equilibria as the discount factor approaches one. This links the long-run formulation to discounted problems and provides both existence results and algorithms for the uncertain multi-player setting.
icml-2026-distributionally-robust-markov.tldr: The paper establishes equilibrium existence and convergent algorithms for robust multi-agent games with long-run average rewards.

paragraphs: FloorplanQA evaluates whether language models can reason consistently about indoor spaces described in structured data. Rooms and their contents are encoded in JSON or XML layouts. This gives the benchmark a symbolic representation of the scene from which models must infer spatial relationships and answer questions about how the space can be used.

The tasks cover measuring distances, determining visibility, finding paths, and placing objects within spatial constraints. They require models to combine layout information with the physical requirements of the question. A successful answer must therefore maintain a coherent understanding of the arrangement, including constraints that can affect movement, visibility, or whether a placement is possible.

Tests across frontier open-source and commercial models show that success on shallow questions can coexist with frequent violations of physical constraints and spatial coherence. Models nevertheless remain mostly robust to small spatial changes. The results identify inconsistent indoor-layout reasoning as a weakness and make FloorplanQA a diagnostic tool for evaluating progress on practical spatial and geometric tasks.
icml-2026-floorplanqa-a-benchmark-for-sp.tldr: FloorplanQA finds that language models often violate spatial constraints when reasoning about symbolically represented indoor layouts.

paragraphs: Biomedical studies often have a small amount of carefully labeled data alongside larger collections without labels. Combining these sources is difficult when they contain unstructured material, such as speech or clinical notes, or record different sets of variables. This paper develops a statistical inference framework designed to use language models despite these mismatches.

The method systematically calibrates pseudo-labels supplied by language models and introduces a prediction-invariance identification strategy. Calibration is central because useful model-generated labels must contribute to parameter estimation without compromising statistical validity. The framework also addresses the requirement that efficiency gains persist when the labeled and unlabeled datasets have different available covariates.

The authors provide theoretical results showing improved estimation efficiency while maintaining statistical validity within their framework. They illustrate the approach through a study of speech data used to identify key biomarkers for Alzheimer’s disease detection. The contribution concerns rigorous population-level inference: it connects the ability of language models to process unstructured observations with a statistical procedure for using their predictions.
icml-2026-language-model-augmented-semi-.tldr: Calibrated language-model pseudo-labels improve semi-supervised statistical estimation while accommodating unstructured data and mismatched covariates.

paragraphs: Gene perturbation experiments can evaluate multiple interventions together, but their budgets remain limited. This paper focuses on finding as many interventions as possible whose effects exceed a chosen threshold. That objective gives value to every newly discovered hit, making the allocation of experiments across promising regions an important part of the problem.

The authors formulate hit discovery as sequential experimental design and propose Probability-of-Hit as the rule for choosing candidates. It ranks each candidate by its posterior probability of exceeding the threshold. This directly aligns experimental selection with the desired outcome. The motivation is that broad exploration can spend resources on low-value regions, while optimization for one global best result can overlook other regions containing useful hits.

The paper proves asymptotic optimality of the proposed approach and evaluates it on synthetic benchmarks and real immunology datasets. Reported gains include up to 6.4% over baselines on the Schmidt IL-2 dataset. The theoretical statement concerns asymptotic behavior, while the experiments provide evidence of useful hit discovery under the evaluated conditions.
icml-2026-many-needles-in-a-haystack-act.tldr: Probability-of-Hit selects experiments by their chance of exceeding a target threshold, aiming to discover many useful perturbations.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning for long-running decisions when the environment may differ from its training dynamics. It proposes Robust Halpern Iteration, a model-free algorithm that targets robust average reward. The goal is to give a finite accounting of how many samples are needed, extending beyond guarantees that describe only eventual behavior.

The development first assumes access to a sampling oracle that accurately estimates worst-case performance. Under a generative-model sampling setting, the authors derive the algorithm’s sample complexity. They then construct an oracle using a K-order multi-level Monte Carlo estimator and show that its bias is lower than that of prior methods.

For uncertainty models including KL and chi-squared divergence sets, the resulting algorithm finds an epsilon-optimal robust policy. Its sample bound scales linearly with the numbers of states and actions, quadratically with the robust optimal span, and nearly as the inverse square of the target error, apart from suppressed factors. The bound asymptotically matches the best complexity for robust average-reward learning under the stated sampling setup.
icml-2026-model-free-robust-average-rewa.tldr: Robust Halpern Iteration provides model-free robust average-reward learning with finite sample guarantees under a generative-model sampling setup.

paragraphs: The paper explores capability access control through modular pretraining. Serving separate models with different knowledge could restrict sensitive capabilities, but training many models is expensive. Gradient-routed auxiliary modules, or GRAM, adds specialized modules during pretraining and selectively directs their updates. Removing a module at inference approximates a model trained with the corresponding data filtered out.

Experiments cover synthetic stories and dual-use material in virology, cybersecurity, nuclear physics, and specialized code. The authors report that module removal disables targeted capabilities while preserving others. In their evaluations, those capabilities also resist recovery through fine-tuning better than capabilities removed by post-hoc unlearning.

A compute-optimal scaling analysis from 50 million to 5 billion parameters finds that data filtering increasingly separates models on removed capabilities while leaving a small gap on retained ones. GRAM closely follows this behavior. Its training cost does not depend on the number of supported capability profiles, producing a fivefold reduction relative to data filtering in the evaluated five-profile setting. These findings support pretraining-time specialization as a practical access-control approach.
icml-2026-modular-pretraining-enables-ac.tldr: GRAM specializes removable modules during pretraining to restrict selected capabilities while preserving others and reducing multi-profile training costs.

paragraphs: Data attribution estimates how a model would change if selected training examples were removed. Influence functions and a single Newton step provide approximations to this change, making their accuracy relevant to interpretability, data valuation, and machine unlearning. The paper develops a new theoretical analysis of these two methods for convex empirical risk minimization.

Previous guarantees rely heavily on global strong convexity and can give pessimistic dependence on model dimension and the number of removed examples. The new analysis uses local conditions instead: strong convexity and sufficient smoothness in a neighborhood of the first Newton step are enough. This narrows the region where the required properties must hold.

For logistic regression with Gaussian features, the authors derive matching upper and lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors. These bounds capture the relevant scaling and explain observed regimes where a Newton step is substantially more accurate than an influence-function estimate. The result clarifies when the two approximations differ and supplies a more precise justification within the analyzed convex setting.
icml-2026-on-the-accuracy-of-newton-step.tldr: Local curvature and smoothness conditions yield sharper attribution guarantees and explain when a Newton step outperforms influence functions.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement learning often learns compact representations in which states are close when their rewards and future transitions are similar. The distance used inside that representation matters. A single fixed distance rule can be too restrictive, while completely unconstrained pairwise distances can reduce the training loss without producing a more useful representation.

PAMD introduces a Pairwise Adaptive Mahalanobis Distance to address this tension. It conditions the distance on the pair of states being compared while retaining a positive-definite mathematical structure. This gives the representation more flexibility than a fixed global norm, together with explicit constraints on how similarity is measured.

The method is designed as a simple addition to existing bisimulation-based algorithms. Experiments on visual MuJoCo continuous-control tasks show substantial improvements in the final performance of several recent algorithms when equipped with PAMD. These results suggest that the geometry used to compare learned states can materially affect control performance, and that making it adaptive while preserving structure is a useful design choice in the evaluated setting.
icml-2026-pamd-structured-adaptive-dista.tldr: PAMD improves visual reinforcement-learning representations with a structured distance that adapts to each pair of states.

paragraphs: Training usually exposes a gradient averaged across a mini-batch, hiding differences among the examples that contributed to it. This paper investigates algorithms that use those individual gradients. It shows that sequence-level architectures and staged programming systems such as JAX provide a practical setting for manipulating per-example gradient computations.

The authors derive implementations of specific per-example and per-token operations with negligible computation or memory overhead. This makes nonlinear operations on gradient information more accessible. Such operations are sensitive to when averaging occurs, so retaining individual contributions can reveal choices that disappear when only the batch average is available.

The paper examines two optimizer components. For signSGD, it shows that where the sign operation is applied is critical, and explains the preferred placement using a signal-to-noise argument. For variants of Adam’s preconditioner, the findings favor dominance by the squared mean of the gradient distribution over its variance. Together, these analyses show how accessible per-example information can support both explanations of optimizer behavior and new algorithm designs.
icml-2026-per-example-gradients-a-new-fr.tldr: Efficient access to per-example gradients reveals consequential choices in signSGD and Adam-style optimizer design.

paragraphs: Predictions can change the outcomes they are supposed to forecast. This paper asks how learning generalizes when such effects alter the observed sample, the wider population, or both. For example, existing app users and potential new users may each react to an app’s predictions, complicating what the existing users reveal about future ones.

The authors incorporate these feedback effects into statistical learning theory and prove generalization bounds for all three cases. Their worst-case intuition distinguishes a sample that deceptively confirms predictions from a population that works against them. They formalize these self-fulfilling and self-negating behaviors through different optimization-based risk formulations in Wasserstein space.

The analysis identifies a fundamental trade-off between changing the world through predictions and learning from the resulting observations. It also shows how retraining on samples already altered by predictions can improve generalization guarantees. Real data on prediction-informed job-training assignments illustrate the bounds. The contribution provides a framework for reasoning about generalization when deployment itself changes the data that learning depends on.
icml-2026-performative-learning-theory-3.tldr: The paper derives generalization bounds for predictions that change their own data and identifies benefits from retraining on affected samples.

paragraphs: Neural networks trained continuously on changing data can gradually lose their ability to learn further. This paper connects that loss of plasticity to the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel and identifies dynamical isometry as a key preservation mechanism. The condition keeps the singular values of each layer’s Jacobian close to one, controlling how changes propagate through layers.

The authors revisit networks that are almost everywhere isometric while still being universal approximators of Lipschitz functions. This establishes compatibility between near-isometry and expressive nonlinear representations. For broader architectures, they propose an efficient regularizer that encourages isometry and identify a mechanism through which it can reactivate dormant ReLU units.

They also introduce AdamO, which separates isometry regularization from gradient updates in an Adam-style optimizer. Earlier plasticity-preserving methods are reinterpreted as addressing only part of isometry. On supervised and reinforcement-learning benchmarks designed to induce plasticity loss, the proposed methods consistently match or outperform existing approaches. The findings connect an architectural property, a regularization method, and an optimizer to preserving continued learning.
icml-2026-preserving-plasticity-in-conti.tldr: Encouraging dynamical isometry helps preserve continual-learning plasticity and motivates a regularizer and the AdamO optimizer.

paragraphs: Private synthetic tabular data methods often treat rows as independent records from different people. Longitudinal data has a different structure: one person can contribute a sequence of events spread across a table. This paper shows that flattening these histories into vectors can preserve individual statistical distributions while failing to preserve how events develop over time.

The proposed framework, PATH, treats the full table as the object to generate and uses privately fine-tuned autoregressive language models. This gives the synthesis process a way to represent sequential dependencies. The goal is to capture coherent trajectories, including long-range relationships that traditional marginal-based methods miss.

In the reported evaluations, PATH reduces distributional distance from real trajectories by more than 60% and state-transition errors by nearly 50% compared with leading marginal mechanisms. It achieves these gains while maintaining similar marginal fidelity. The findings demonstrate why matching statistics of individual variables is insufficient for longitudinal synthesis, and provide evidence that modeling the table’s temporal structure improves the realism of generated histories.
icml-2026-privately-fine-tuned-llms-pres.tldr: PATH uses privately fine-tuned language models to generate longitudinal tables with more faithful trajectories and state transitions.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how diffusion language models can assess their own reasoning without a known correct answer. Its starting hypothesis is geometric: valid reasoning trajectories behave like stable attractors in high-density regions of the learned distribution, while invalid trajectories tend to drift away. The authors turn that hypothesis into a measurable consistency test.

Bidirectional Manifold Consistency masks a generated sequence and then reconstructs it, measuring stability across that cycle. The metric requires neither training nor supervised labels. Its purpose is to provide an internal signal about whether a solution is valid by testing how reliably the model returns to the generated sequence.

Experiments explore three uses. The score distinguishes valid solutions without ground-truth answers, guides rejection resampling during inference, and supplies a dense reward for alignment. In the alignment setting, it turns sparse outcome supervision into finer-grained guidance and supports improvement beyond standard baselines. These findings support geometric stability as an empirical indicator of correctness in the studied diffusion models, building on the paper’s proposed hypothesis.
icml-2026-reasoning-on-the-manifold-bidi.tldr: A masking-and-reconstruction consistency score helps diffusion language models assess reasoning, guide resampling, and obtain finer-grained alignment rewards.

paragraphs: ScenePilot generates difficult driving scenarios for testing autonomous vehicles. Its target is a specific region of difficulty: situations that are physically solvable in principle but still cause the deployed driving system to fail. This matters because a crash in a physically impossible situation offers a different testing signal from failure in an avoidable one.

The framework formulates scenario generation as constrained multi-objective reinforcement learning. It combines an RSS-derived physical-feasibility score with an autonomous-vehicle risk predictor learned online. A feasibility-aware shield acts at individual steps to keep exploration near the physical boundary while avoiding infeasible artifacts. These components jointly direct the generator toward challenging, physically valid situations.

On SafeBench with multiple planners, the authors report collision rates higher by 6.2 percentage points while preserving physical validity. They also find that adversarial fine-tuning on these scenarios consistently reduces downstream crash rates. The results support using physically solvable failures both to expose weaknesses in deployed planners and to generate training cases that improve performance in the evaluated setting.
icml-2026-scenepilot-controllable-bounda.tldr: ScenePilot generates physically solvable driving scenarios that expose planner failures and support training that reduces subsequent crashes.

paragraphs: SOTAlign studies how to connect pretrained vision and language models when only a small number of matched image-text examples is available. Its motivation is the hypothesis that separately trained models can develop related representations of the world. The paper asks whether this relationship can support alignment using abundant unpaired data and limited direct supervision.

The method has two stages. A linear teacher first uses the paired examples to recover a coarse shared geometry. An optimal-transport-based divergence then refines the alignment with unpaired images and text. This second stage transfers relationships among representations while avoiding excessive constraints on the target space.

The authors report robust joint embeddings across different datasets and encoder combinations, with significant improvements over supervised and semi-supervised baselines. These findings support the usefulness of unpaired data for alignment in the proposed setting. The approach makes limited image-text matches serve as an initial guide, then uses the structure of larger unpaired collections to improve the connection between the two modalities.
icml-2026-sotalign-semi-supervised-align.tldr: SOTAlign combines a small paired dataset with optimal transport on unpaired data to align pretrained vision and language representations.

paragraphs: TerraBind investigates whether predicting how a small molecule binds to a protein requires expensive all-atom structure generation. It uses a coarser representation containing protein C-beta atoms and ligand heavy atoms. Pretrained molecular encoders and ESM-2 protein embeddings provide additional information within a multimodal architecture.

The learned representations feed a diffusion-free optimization module for generating ligand poses and a likelihood-based module for predicting binding affinity. On structure benchmarks, TerraBind matches diffusion-based baselines in pose accuracy. The authors report 26-fold faster inference than state-of-the-art methods and affinity improvements of 16–20% in Pearson correlation over Boltz-2 on CASP16 and a private dataset covering 18 assays.

The affinity module also produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, which matter when prioritizing compounds using uncertain predictions. It supports continual learning and a hedged batch-selection strategy. In simulated drug-discovery cycles, that strategy achieves sixfold greater affinity improvement than greedy approaches. These results support the usefulness of coarse structural representations for the evaluated prediction tasks and distinguish the simulation finding from experimentally demonstrated discovery outcomes.
icml-2026-terrabind-fast-and-accurate-bi.tldr: TerraBind uses coarse structures for faster protein-ligand prediction, improving affinity estimates while matching diffusion baselines on ligand poses.

paragraphs: Posterior sampling uses a generative model to produce outputs consistent with observations or desired conditions. This paper develops that capability for discrete diffusion, which can model both text and images. It addresses difficulties in existing methods, including sparse guidance signals, restrictive continuous relaxations, and the dimensionality problems of split Gibbs sampling.

Anchored Posterior Sampling introduces two components. Quantized expectation supplies gradient-like guidance in discrete embedding space, giving the sampling process a directional signal. Anchored remasking provides adaptive decoding. Together, these mechanisms are designed to guide generation within the discrete framework while overcoming the stated weaknesses of earlier posterior samplers.

On standard image benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance among discrete diffusion samplers for both linear and nonlinear inverse problems. They also demonstrate stylization and text-guided editing without additional training. Applying the approach to a large diffusion language model consistently improves question answering. These evaluations show the method operating across image reconstruction, controllable image generation, and language tasks, supporting its intended generality.
icml-2026-test-time-anchoring-for-discre.tldr: Anchored Posterior Sampling combines discrete guidance and adaptive remasking to improve image inverse problems, editing, and question answering.

paragraphs: Satisficing bandits ask a learner to find and use any option whose expected reward exceeds a known threshold. When such an option exists, earlier work gives regret bounds that do not grow with time. However, those guarantees become worse when an option’s expected reward is close to the threshold.

The paper focuses on cases where the best option exceeds the threshold by only a small amount relative to the gaps separating options from the best. It introduces a refined regret notion and an algorithm called uncertain-UCB. The resulting satisficing pseudo-regret bound depends on the individual gaps and only logarithmically on the inverse excess of the best option above the threshold.

When no option exceeds the threshold, the algorithm recovers standard pseudo-regret guarantees. The authors also prove a near-matching lower bound in the small-excess regime, identifying difficulty that any algorithm must face there. Together, the results sharpen the achievable guarantees and explain how the reward gaps govern the cost of finding an acceptable option.
icml-2026-understanding-the-gaps-in-sati.tldr: Uncertain-UCB sharpens satisficing-bandit regret guarantees when the best option barely exceeds the acceptance threshold.
